data.title: Middle East Eye: The paper trail that leads from the UAE to a dead boy in Sudan
data.author: Ahmed Ismat Ahmed
data.summary:
The paper trail that leads from the UAE to a dead boy in Sudan
Submitted by
Ahmed Ismat Ahmed
on

The RSF killed Osama, my little brother's 12-year-old best friend. This is what made it possible
Osama (r) and his best friend Mohammed, pictured a week before the war in Sudan began in April 2023 (Ahmed Ismat Ahmed/MEE)
On
Osama was my younger brother’s best friend. He was 12. The Rapid Support Forces killed him when they attacked a town in al-Jazira state, Sudan, in 2023.
The two of them used to share the same bicycle - one pedalling, the other running beside it, hand on the seat. Then one of them simply stopped existing.
After the Khartoum sit-in was broken in the spring of 2019 and the resistance committees - nationwide groups of local activists of which I was a part - moved into the neighbourhoods, a few of us found ourselves guarding wool.
Eid was coming. Families who could still afford it had bought sheep. When the slaughtering was done, the wool was left in the open lot where we used to meet.
Someone said it was a waste to sell it in small piles for almost nothing. Someone else said the locality had not touched the streetlights on our main road in months. Children fell when it rained. Old people stopped walking to the mosque after dark because they could not see the path.
We gathered the wool and took turns sitting with it at night. When the money came - folded, counted twice - we sat down and wrote it into a cheap notebook with a blue cover.
I learned early that there are two kinds of paperwork. They do not answer to the same people
Different hands. The wool money. The cost of the generator. Who had counted. The names of the boys who brought something. The phone numbers of mothers to call if something went wrong.
Nobody set out to make an archive. It became one because no other archive had space for us.

data.title: Middle East Eye: How Morocco is becoming Israel's security hub in Africa
data.author: Ahmed Alqarout
data.summary:
How Morocco is becoming Israel's security hub in Africa

on

Rabat offers its Abraham Accords partners an industrial safe haven, away from missiles and sanctions
An Israeli soldier launches an Elbit unmanned aerial vehicle, used for surveillance, near the border with Gaza on 30 September 2025 (Jack Guez/AFP)
Off
At the Marrakech Air Show last month, Israel’s defence ministry opened its first official pavilion in Morocco.
Eight Israeli firms, among them the state-owned Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) and Rafael, showed drones, loitering munitions and air defence systems, while Elbit’s Moroccan joint venture announced that it would deliver turrets to the Moroccan army from March 2027.
Also at the air show, the UAE’s defence group Edge signed a contract to arm Morocco’s drones.
The event coincided with the anniversary of 7 October, which drew protesters to a vigil outside parliament in Rabat. Events were called in some 30 Moroccan cities, urging the government to drop new measures aimed at further normalising ties with Israel. BDS Morocco called for a boycott of the Marrakech show.
The air show illustrates how, since joining the Abraham Accords in 2020, Morocco has moved from buying Israeli weapons to building them. The war on Gaza accelerated that partnership, as global boycotts and sanctions against Israel expanded.
In Europe, Spain cancelled €1.2bn ($1.3bn) of Israeli military contracts, and France barred Israel from the Eurosatory defence exhibition.
The war with Iran further exposed Israeli and Emirati industries. Iran said it struck Rafael and IAI sites, along with a drone supplier, and Emirates Global Aluminium’s Abu Dhabi plant suffered significant damage.
Morocco offers its Abraham Accords partners an industrial safe haven, away from missiles and sanctions, and its coordination with Israel now spans production, intelligence, training, weapons testing, shipping and policing in Gaza.

data.author: MEE staff

Mohamed Yusuf was reportedly run over multiple times with his own vehicle after a passenger said he disliked his Muslim name
A screenshot of a GoFundMe fundraiser launched to support Mohamed Yusuf, the Somali-American Uber driver who was the victim of a suspected hate crime in Minnesota
Off
A Somali-American Uber driver is fighting for his life after being strangled and repeatedly run over with his own vehicle, allegedly by a passenger in Minnesota, in an attack his family believes was motivated by anti-Muslim hatred.
Mohamed Yusuf was working in Hopkins, a suburb of Minneapolis, early on Saturday when a passenger allegedly asked him his name before telling him he did not like the name "Mohamed".
According to Yusuf's relatives, the passenger then allegedly choked him from behind, seized control of his vehicle and ran him over multiple times.
"He was run over multiple times with his own vehicle," Yusuf's son, Mustafa Osman, told The Somali Brief.
Yusuf was reportedly found in a ditch nearly a mile away, suffering from broken legs and ribs, two collapsed lungs, a spinal injury and internal bleeding.
He remains hospitalised in a coma, according to his family.
Hopkins police confirmed that officers responding to a report of a suspicious vehicle at around 1.20am on Saturday discovered a seriously injured man and subsequently took a male suspect into custody.
According to the Times of India, arrest records show that a man identified as Samit Apurva Patel was taken into custody by Hopkins Police on 14 November on a first-degree assault charge.
However, authorities have not confirmed whether Patel's arrest is connected to Yusuf's assault or publicly identified the suspect in the case.
Police have also not established a motive or confirmed whether the incident is being investigated as a hate crime.

Almost a year ago to the day, Abbott announced that he was designating the Muslim Brotherhood as well as Cair as foreign terrorist organisations and transnational criminal organisations.
As a result, both groups were barred "from purchasing or acquiring land" in Texas.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iran still retains up to 2,500 ballistic missiles: Report
data.author: Hossam Desouky
data.summary:
Iran still retains up to 2,500 ballistic missiles: Report
The US believes Iran has between 1,500 and 2,500 ballistic missiles in its arsenal, a substantial number that contradicts the Trump administration’s claims that Iran has been militarily decimated.
The US intelligence community ranked the assessment “low confidence”, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday, but the American estimate generally aligns with Israel’s, which says Iran has more than 1,500 missiles.
President Donald Trump has regularly characterised Iran as a defeated and broken nation. Full-scale war between the US and Iran has subsided, but the two are still exchanging strikes.
Iran attacked US military assets in Bahrain twice in the last week in response to US strikes on its own military infrastructure. Iran also said on Monday that it struck two vessels in the Strait of Hormuz with mines, sinking one Very Large Crude Carrier, known as a VLCC.
The fact that Iran retains a vast arsenal of ballistic missiles may be why the US has refrained from relaunching strikes on Iran, despite Trump boasting that the US had “won” the war and achieved a “93 percent victory” over the Islamic Republic.

Mamdani to disband special NYPD unit deployed during pro-Palestinian protests

The unit faced widespread criticism for its aggressive tactics and had high rates of civilian complaints
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani holds a news conference at City Hall in New York City, on 13 November 2026 (Adam Gray/Getty Images via AFP)
Off
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Monday that he will keep his campaign promise to disband the New York Police Department's Strategic Response Group (SRG) and replace it with “de-escalation groups”.
The armour-clad SRG is made up of 500 highly trained NYPD officers who have become infamous for their “crowd control tactics” and mass arrests during protests in New York City, where they use batons, tear gas, pepper spray and other “de-escalation” weapons on disruptive protesters.
The group came under particular scrutiny during pro-Palestine protests during the height of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and campus protests led by the student movement that started at Columbia University.
New York Civil Liberties Union executive director Donna Lieberman applauded the move and said, “These important changes will make protests safer and allow more New Yorkers to raise their voices”.
Police commissioner Jessica Tisch told ABC7 that despite the disbandment of the SRG, “New Yorkers can expect in crowd control type situations to see the very same response that they are accustomed to" and that "nothing would change about the way that the NYPD responds to crowd control conditions”.
But a press release from the NYC mayor's office says there will be significant change in how police interact with protesters.
“This overhaul will transform how the City prepares for and responds to protests, placing communication, de-escalation and civilian coordination at the center of our approach, while protecting New Yorkers’ constitutional right to protest,” the statement said.
